data.title: KuCoin Advances Australian Engagement at CryptoCon Sydney, Spotlighting Global Infrastructure and Local Accountability
data.description:
SYDNEY, Nov. 28, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- KuCoin highlighted the importance of connecting global exchange capabilities with local responsibilities at CryptoCon Sydney at ICC Sydney. During the panel "Global Infrastructure, Local Accountability: Where Exchanges Fit in Crypto's Next Phase," KuCoin CMO Skylar W and Managing Director of KuCoin in Australia James Pinch discussed how exchanges can respond to broader financial needs through infrastructure investment, market-specific governance and local delivery. They were joined by Zach Ahmajani, Head of Operations at KuCoin in Australia, in a discussion moderated by Lydia Ward, Growth Manager of KuCoin in Australia.

Skylar described an industry in which trading volume, liquidity and asset selection remain important, but expectations increasingly extend to the infrastructure and operating standards behind those services. She connected KuCoin's investment in security and transparency through its $2 Billion Trust Project with the development of its global compliance framework and institutional services. "Global capabilities are the starting point. What matters is how the product works locally, with clear responsibilities from day one," said Skylar W. Her remarks also highlighted continued work on trading architecture and security infrastructure to support performance and resilience as financial activity becomes more demanding.

During the discussion, Skylar also introduced KuCoin 5.0 as an example of how those investments translate into tangible improvements for users. Launched under the "Trust, Built-in." initiative, the platform-wide upgrade offers distinct Lite and Pro experiences and a single point of access to AI assistance across the platform. It also introduces a Unified Trading Account that allows eligible users at VIP1 and above to manage funds and trade across spot, margin and futures from one account.

James brought that discussion back to the tasks users need to complete. Drawing on a focus group involving people who had purchased crypto in the previous 12 to 24 months, he described participants using digital assets to pay vendors and send money overseas. While those observations reflected the group rather than all users, they illustrated why exchanges need to consider the full journey of moving and using funds. "Some of the people we spoke to were buying crypto because they had a payment or transfer to make," said James Pinch. "Banks and exchanges each have a role, and the opportunity is to improve how those services meet the needs of people and businesses."

The discussion connected these changing needs with a practical requirement: global infrastructure must translate into services that reflect the market they serve. For KuCoin, that means combining technology and product expertise with local understanding, clearly identifying service-provider responsibilities and distinguishing global capabilities from services available through the relevant entity. Security measures, reserve disclosures and independent assessments contribute to that approach by giving users information about platform practices within defined scopes.

This emphasis on accountability extended to "The Future of Finance in Australia: A Government & Regulatory Roundtable," where James Kwan, KuCoin Australia's legal lead, joined representatives from the Australian Taxation Office (ATO), the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC), and DECA. The session explored priorities for the responsible development of Australia's digital asset market, placing regulatory dialogue and governance alongside the industry's technology and product development.

KuCoin's participation followed the opening of its Australian programme with Global Brand Ambassador Adam Scott on 23 November. Building on its collaboration with the convention in 2025, its three-year partnership with CryptoCon Sydney provides an ongoing forum for engagement with Australian users and industry partners. Together with its Sydney office and local leadership team established in 2025, the partnership supports KuCoin's long-term approach to bringing global resources into services shaped by local expertise and needs.

About KuCoin

Founded in 2017, KuCoin is a leading global crypto platform built on trust and security, serving over 45 million users across 200+ countries and regions. Known for its reliability and user-first approach, the platform builds trust into every layer of the user experience, combining advanced technology, deep liquidity, and strong security safeguards to deliver a seamless trading experience. KuCoin globally provides access to 1,000+ digital assets through a broad product suite and remains committed to building a secure, transparent, compliant, and user-centric ecosystem for the future of finance, backed by SOC 2 Type II, ISO/IEC 27001:2022, ISO/IEC 27701:2019, ISO 22301:2019 and ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certifications. In recent years, KuCoin has continued to strengthen its global compliance foundation, marked by key milestones including AUSTRAC registration in Australia, a MiCA license in Europe, and regulatory progress in other markets.

Learn more at www.kucoin.com.

data.title: Gold And Palladium: The Comeback Meets Its First Test
data.description:
Remember how things looked on Wednesday? The bears had plenty of reasons to celebrate.

Gold had broken below a major psychological barrier. Silver had challenged an important weekly Fibonacci retracement. Platinum, palladium, and copper were reaching increasingly deep support levels.

It wasn't exactly a comfortable picture for the bulls. But apparently, someone forgot to tell the buyers that the week was already over.

And what a comeback they're attempting!

Fresh bullish gaps have appeared across the metals during the past two sessions, and buyers are now challenging several levels that had previously belonged firmly to the bears.

Yet there's a catch. Reclaiming lost support is one thing. Breaking through the resistance left behind by the previous selloff is another.

Today, gold and palladium provide two particularly interesting examples of that challenge. One is attempting to recover after losing a major psychological barrier. The other is fighting back after briefly falling beneath an important historical low.

Let's see what their charts are telling us.

Gold (GC.F) - A Bullish Comeback Meets Its First Major Test

Gold's buyers have certainly made their presence felt. Remember Wednesday?

The yellow metal had plunged below 3500, challenging an important historical support combination and raising the possibility of another decline toward the 3300 area, but the bears couldn't maintain their advantage.

Gold recovered above 3500, invalidating the immediate intraday breakdown beneath that psychological barrier. Then Thursday's Asian session brought a fresh bullish gap at 3535.80-3583.60. Even though sellers subsequently attempted to push prices lower, the gap wasn't completely filled.

And today's reaction has been considerably stronger.

Gold increased to 3683.65, challenging the bearish gap from November 20 at 3633-3685, which means buyers came within just 1.35 of its upper boundary!

What Could Strengthen the Bullish Case?

The first requirement is a convincing daily close above the recovered support levels.

A Friday close above 3535 would reinforce the invalidation of Wednesday's breakdown beneath 3500 and improve the short-term technical picture. It would also support the developing recovery from the historical green support area marked on the weekly chart.

However, reclaiming the lower boundary of the red declining channel on D1 is a separate technical test. That boundary, together with the November 20 bearish gap, continues to present an important obstacle. If buyers manage to overcome this resistance combination, the recovery would gain a much stronger technical foundation.

Conversely, another rejection beneath these barriers could leave gold vulnerable to renewed selling pressure and with the weekly RSI still relatively weak and Stochastic deeply oversold, the broader structure deserves particular attention.

Daily Takeaway: supports: the bullish gap at 3535.80-3583.60, followed by the psychological 3500 barrier. Key resistance: the November 20 bearish gap at 3633-3685 and the nearby declining-channel boundary. Closing above these barriers would strengthen the recovery scenario.

Bottom Line: Gold has challenged Wednesday's bearish breakdown, but the next important achievement would be converting this impressive rebound into a confirmed recovery above overhead resistance.

Palladium (PA.F) - A Powerful Gap and a Historical Level Reclaimed

Palladium's bulls have delivered one of the week's most dramatic responses.

After Wednesday's decline carried prices through another Fibonacci objective and below the August 2024 low at 813.50, the bearish outlook appeared increasingly demanding for buyers. However, Thursday brought a remarkable change.

A substantial bullish opening gap appeared at 772-859, providing the foundation for a powerful recovery attempt and on Friday, buyers extended their offensive.

Palladium reached 907.75, entering the bearish gap from November 20 at 906-918. Although the recovery subsequently retreated toward 877, the latest price remains above an especially important historical reference. The August 2024 low at 813.50 has been reclaimed, which is potentially significant.

What Would Confirm the Improvement?

If palladium finishes Friday's session above 813.50, it would strengthen the case that the earlier breakdown beneath that historical low has been invalidated. A weekly close above the same level would provide additional confirmation. That would leave buyers with a stronger foundation for another attempt to overcome the 906-918 resistance zone. Beyond that, attention would turn toward the previously broken lower boundary of the red declining wedge visible on W1.

Successfully reclaiming that weekly boundary would be another important step in repairing the technical structure and could eventually open the door to a challenge of the psychological 1000 barrier.

For now, the weekly trend remains weak and the market is still emerging from deeply oversold conditions, but the recovery above 813.50 gives buyers a meaningful level to defend.

Daily Takeaway: key support: 813.50, together with the bullish-gap area at 772-859. Resistances: 906-918, followed by the broken weekly wedge boundary and potentially 1000. Friday's close above 813.50 would strengthen the bullish recovery scenario.

Bottom Line: Palladium has staged a powerful counterattack but transforming that rebound into a sustained technical improvement will require buyers to reclaim more than one previously broken resistance level.

What About the Other Four Markets?

U.S. Dollar - The Bulls Defend Support, but Resistance Still Awaits

While the metals are recovering, the dollar remains inside its orange consolidation. Buyers have successfully defended an important bullish-gap support area, but another bearish gap and a broader weekly resistance combination continue to stand in their way.

Silver - The Bulls Return to the Battlefield

After a dramatic decline earlier this week, silver has reclaimed important support and challenged a bearish gap from November 20. The next question is whether buyers can maintain that improvement and push through the resistance separating them from another psychological barrier.

Platinum - Can the Bulls Reclaim the Weekly Channel?

Platinum has also benefited from renewed buying interest. Its recovery has carried prices back above an important weekly channel boundary and toward nearby daily resistance. Friday's closing result could help determine whether the latest rebound has a stronger technical foundation.

Copper - Buyers Defend an Important Historical Low

Copper has staged its own counterattack, reclaiming several Fibonacci extensions intraday after an unsuccessful attempt to break an important historical low. However, another resistance area remains overhead, making the next closing signals particularly interesting.

Today's Anna's Trading Lab Premium follows the latest developments across all six markets, including the support levels buyers are attempting to reclaim, the resistance areas standing in their way, and the technical conditions that could shape next week's trading. The complete edition also includes our Friday's Cheat Sheet, bringing together the key levels and scenarios worth watching as the market approaches December.

Final Thought - The First Test of a Comeback

There's a detail worth noticing in both gold and palladium today.

Buyers have managed to stage substantial recoveries, reaching resistance areas created during the previous selloff, but on our latest charts, both metals have already retreated from their intraday highs.

That gives us a particularly useful way to evaluate the strength of this comeback. It's not just about how far prices managed to rise. It's also about how much of that recovery buyers can preserve when sellers return near familiar resistance.

Friday's closing candles may help answer that question, while the next attempt to challenge those overhead barriers could reveal whether the bulls are building lasting momentum or still struggling to regain lost territory.

After all, the strength of a comeback isn't always measured by its most impressive moment. Sometimes, it's revealed by what buyers manage to hold onto afterward.

data.title: Ignore Friday's Short Session. Monday Is When The Year Gets Priced.
data.description:
Wall Street loves a holiday bounce because the charts look clean and the headlines write themselves. On Black Friday the whole show wraps by 1 p.m. Eastern, and the trading floor feels more like a skeleton crew than a real market.

My take is simple. This short session does not decide how the rest of the year goes. The people who move real size are already looking past it. Monday is when full desks come back, the order books regain depth, and the next stretch of economic data starts answering questions this market still has not settled.

A half day is not a verdict

U.S. stocks were closed Thursday for Thanksgiving, and Friday is the classic early close. You get about three and a half hours instead of the usual six and a half. Volume on this day often runs near half of a normal session, and sometimes lower than that.

That thin book is the whole point. When fewer institutional players are present, a modest order can push a stock farther than it would on an ordinary Tuesday in March. Spreads widen and false breakouts show up. A green close can feel like renewed confidence when it is really just a quiet room with fewer people arguing over price.

History leans a little green on Black Friday over the long haul, and that is fine as trivia. It is a weak foundation for a year-end investment thesis. In a high-fear stretch, a short day can still swing hard if a headline lands, which the Omicron scare a few years back already proved. The calendar does not make the market honest. Participation does. So if futures are ripping higher into the open, enjoy the color. Do not build your story for the rest of 2026 on three and a half hours of holiday traffic.

What this week already told us

This market staggered into the turkey after a brutal stretch. The S&P 500 had already slipped more than 10% off the early October high and into correction territory. Artificial intelligence names did a lot of the damage. Nvidia's (NVDA) leadership fight, Anthropic's rough first days as a public company, and a broader argument over how much of the AI capital spending is real end demand versus expensive hope all hit at once. Then the holiday week tried to put air back in the tires. By the time Friday futures lit up, the major indexes were looking at a multi-day rebound on the order of about 4% for the week.

That rebound matters as a mood check. It does not close the case. Can the AI complex hold when the full crowd is trading again, and can earnings keep up with the capital thrown at chips and data centers? Holiday liquidity is a terrible place to answer either question.

Monday is the first honest session

Full hours return Monday, November 30. That is when the real auction starts again. I do not mean Monday is magic. I mean it is the first day the people who move size are back in their seats with a full week on the board. Seasonal studies often show the Monday after Thanksgiving giving back some of Friday's cheer once volume returns.

This year the calendar after the holiday is heavier than the leftovers. Next week brings manufacturing and services surveys, private payrolls color, and the November jobs report on December 4. Economists polled around the wires have been looking for something like 90,000 jobs and an unemployment rate near 4.1%. Those figures feed straight into the Federal Reserve meeting on December 8 and 9. Futures markets have been pricing a quarter-point rate increase as a near lock, roughly in the high-90% range on the CME FedWatch tool. The fight is less about whether policymakers move and more about how hard they talk about 2027.

That stack is the real year-end machine: labor strength or softness, wage pressure, and how the committee sounds about inflation that has refused to settle. Layer AI drama back on top. Early December hearings around Nvidia's returned chief executive can reopen the confidence debate overnight. Thin Friday prices will not survive that kind of week if the story turns again.

How I am watching it

As for me, I am treating Friday like weather, not climate. I want Monday and Tuesday to hold the rebound with real volume, not just another gap that fades by lunch. I want market breadth, not only a handful of megacap stocks dragging the averages. I want the jobs report to either confirm a still-firm economy the Fed can lean against or show enough cooling that investors can debate the path without another panic. Holiday futures strength is cheap courage. Holding gains into a Federal Reserve week is different.

None of that is a recommendation to chase Friday's open or to fade a green candle because the calendar says so. It is a reminder that markets tell the truth when capital is present and the next hard data is on the table.

Bottom Line

Black Friday's short session is a thin holiday read with an early closing bell. The rest of 2026 gets priced when full desks return Monday and the market has to live with jobs week and a December Fed that is almost certainly raising rates again.

data.title: EU Commission Simplifies EU Taxonomy Criteria To Classify Sustainable Activities
data.description:
The European Commission announced the adoption of two new delegated acts aimed at simplifying requirements for companies to demonstrate that activities and projects can be classified as environmentally sustainable under the EU Taxonomy, the framework designed to help facilitate access to sustainability-labeled financing and investment from sustainability-focused funds.

The EU Taxonomy, part of the EU Sustainable Finance Framework, is aimed at helping to facilitate the flow of capital towards activities that contribute to the EU’s sustainability goals. The taxonomy establishes a classification system for economic activities that play key roles in contributing to a series of defined environmental objectives, with criteria for inclusion requiring an activity to contribute substantially to at least one of the objectives, and to do no significant harm (DNSH) to the other objectives.

The EU Taxonomy regulation entered into force in 2020, and since 2021 capital investments into taxonomy‑aligned activities have amounted to €1.2 trillion. The new revisions follow a set of significant simplification measures implemented in the taxonomy as part of 2025’s Omnibus I process, which included dramatically reducing the number of datapoints in the taxonomy’s reporting templates, and exempting companies from assessing taxonomy alignment for non-material activities.

According to the Commission, the new delegated acts, which include revisions to the Climate and Environmental Delegated Acts, target areas in which experience has indicated that requirements are overly complex, duplicative or difficult to apply consistently, with the revisions designed to make the taxonomy’s criteria clearer and easier to apply by removing unnecessary or duplicative requirements, aligning them with updated EU legislation and technological developments, and clarifying how companies can demonstrate compliance.

The new delegated acts introduce a wide range of simplification measures, spanning Taxonomy criteria for activities in sectors including forestry, manufacturing, energy, transport, construction and real estate, as well as cross-sector changes aimed at making it easier for companies to demonstrate compliance with the Taxonomy’s “Do No Significant Harm” (DNSH) criteria.

Examples of the revisions introduced by the Commission include expanding the criteria for building renovations to qualify as sustainable by allowing for an improvement of two energy performance certificate (EPC) classes, exempting the renovation of individual homes and apartments from circular economy and certain pollution prevention requirements, introducing greater flexibility in physical climate risk assessments and exempting mobile assets from such assessments, and enabling companies to demonstrate compliance with water and biodiversity protection criteria through existing environmental permits and other evidence of regulatory compliance.

The revised delegated acts will be submitted for a four-month scrutiny period by the EU Parliament and Council, with the changes anticipated to begin applying from January 1, 2028.

data.title: The Next AI Giants Could Be Tiny
data.description:
In the 1960s, computers were so big and expensive that only governments, universities and the largest corporations could afford them.

Then came the personal computer. And within a few decades, billions of people had access to computing power that was once reserved for some of the world’s most powerful institutions.

It was one of the most important technological developments of our lifetimes. And it created enormous fortunes for investors who saw it coming.

Today, I believe we’re approaching a similar moment with artificial intelligence.

You see, up until now, the AI boom has largely revolved around a handful of tech giants building massive data centers.

But I’m starting to see evidence that the next wave of AI investment could take us in the opposite direction.

And that could open up an entirely new market for some of America’s smallest technology companies.

The Push for AI Independence

When you ask ChatGPT a question, your request is typically sent over the internet to a data center where powerful computer chips process it and send you back an answer.

I’m not particularly concerned about where my data goes when I ask ChatGPT to help me plan a vacation or recommend a good book.

But consider what happens when a pharmaceutical company wants to use AI to develop a new drug. Or when an aerospace company wants to use it to design a more efficient jet engine.

These companies spend billions of dollars developing products that they don’t want their competitors to know anything about.

And they’re understandably concerned about sending that information outside their own computer networks.

Even the legal protections surrounding that information are being called into question.

Earlier this year, a federal judge ruled that a defendant’s conversations with the AI chatbot Claude weren’t protected by attorney-client privilege.

While companies can use cloud-based AI securely, cases like this help explain why some businesses want more control over their data.

And I’m hearing more about this from some of the biggest names in the AI industry.

In a recent letter to shareholders, Palantir Technologies (Nasdaq: PLTR) CEO Alex Karp wrote: “A global movement is emerging. The revolution for independence and AI sovereignty is now well underway.”

AI sovereignty is essentially the ability to control your own AI systems and the data they use.

For a business, that could mean running AI on its own computers to keep sensitive information within its private network.

And thanks to some recent advances in AI technology, that’s becoming a much more practical option.

You see, there’s a big difference between training an AI model and actually using one.

Training a powerful AI model can require thousands of expensive computer chips working together for months at a time. But once that model has been trained, it can often run on far less powerful equipment.

Using a trained AI model to perform a task is known as inference.

And as you can see in the chart below, spending on AI inference is projected to overtake spending on AI training by 2030.

Source: Bloomberg Intelligence, Morgan Stanley Investment Management, August 2025.
Recreated using approximate chart values.

That’s particularly exciting because inference can often take place outside the massive data centers where AI models are trained.

And researchers are getting better at developing smaller AI models that can perform specific tasks extremely well.

A hospital, for example, doesn’t necessarily need an AI model that can write poetry, translate dozens of languages and explain quantum physics. It might simply need one that can analyze medical images or help doctors review patient records.

Running that AI locally could allow the hospital to process sensitive patient information without sending it to an outside company.

There are other advantages, too.

A manufacturer using AI to inspect products as they move down an assembly line needs to identify defects in real time.

Processing that information locally can reduce delays and allow the system to keep working even if its internet connection goes down.

Then there’s the challenge of building enough data centers to meet the world’s demand for AI.

As I’ve written about before, communities across America are pushing back against data center construction because of concerns about electricity prices, water consumption and the strain these facilities put on local infrastructure.

And even when developers find communities willing to welcome them, getting enough electricity to power these enormous facilities can take years.

So there’s a growing incentive to find ways to bring computing power directly to the businesses that need it.

And the potential market is enormous.

Morgan Stanley estimates that AI could eventually create a $40 trillion market opportunity.

Even a small fraction of that could represent an enormous opportunity for companies supplying businesses with their own AI infrastructure.

Here’s My Take

I still expect the world’s biggest tech companies to spend enormous amounts of money building data centers over the next several years.

But I also believe that we’re going to see a lot more businesses invest in their own AI infrastructure.

And that has exciting implications for investors.

Think back to the personal computer revolution. IBM (IBM) was already a giant in the computer industry when companies like Microsoft (MSFT) and Apple (AAPL) were just getting started.

But the emergence of a whole new market for computers gave these smaller companies an opportunity to become giants in their own right.

I’ve been researching several small technology companies that are developing solutions to help businesses gain greater control over their artificial intelligence.

And on Monday, I’ll show you how a remarkable invention from 20 years ago could help make it possible.

data.title: Can Record Black Friday Spending Lift Amazon Stock?
data.description:
Amazon (AMZN - Free Report) enters Black Friday with U.S. shoppers expected to spend a record $12.9 billion online, up 9.2% year over year, according to Adobe Analytics.

Furthermore, Cyber Monday spending is projected to rise 6.2% to $15.1 billion. This comes as the National Retail Federation forecasts U.S. retail sales for the November and December holiday shopping period to be up 4.2% and poised to cross $1 trillion for the first time.

That said, investors are certainly wondering if that spending can give AMZN stock a further boost.

Amazon's Holiday Sales Outlook & Growth Trajectory

Amazon is offering millions of deals through Nov. 30, with extra releases on Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Its AI shopping assistant (Alexa for Shopping) can also track prices and automatically buy eligible items at a shopper’s target price.

Management’s published outlook covers the full fourth quarter, with sales projected at $240 billion to $247 billion. The Zacks Consensus calls for Q4 sales to rise 15% YoY to $245.44 billion and quarterly EPS expected to climb over 26% to $2.47.

Based on Zacks projections, Amazon’s top line is now expected to expand by nearly 16% in fiscal 2026 and FY27, with the tech giant on track to bring in well over $1 trillion in annual sales by FY28 if this growth rate were to persist.

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

More intriguingly, full-year EPS is forecasted to spike 80% in FY26 to $12.89 from $7.17 last year. However, it’s noteworthy that FY27 EPS is projected to decline 16% to $10.78 amid heavy spending on AI infrastructure, with Amazon projecting about $220 billion in CapEx this year.

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

AMZN Shows Relative Strength

Notably, AMZN shares are up roughly 6% in November despite the broader tech selloff, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq have both fallen 5%, led by Nvidia’s (NVDA - Free Report) nearly 30% decline.  

Leading to the favorable resistance is that Amazon offers exposure to retail, advertising, and AI in a single holding. This comes as AWS cloud computing sales grew 39% YoY in Q3 to $46 billion, and Anthropic (ANT - Free Report) is expanding the use of Amazon’s custom Trainium chips for training and running its Claude AI models.

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

Conclusion & Strategic Thoughts

Amazon stock currently lands a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold). The mix of retail, advertising, and cloud computing makes AMZN a compelling long-term holding, but the projected earnings decline in FY27 may still make it worth waiting for a better entry point.

Although AMZN trades at a reasonable 23X forward earnings multiple, investors may want clearer evidence that growing demand for AWS’s AI services can eventually lift free cash flow as Amazon ramps up infrastructure spending.

data.title: Gold And Silver Crash? Mark Thornton Says The Fed Will Blink
data.description:
On the November 27, 2026, episode of the Money Metals podcast, host Mike Maharrey interviewed Dr. Mark Thornton, an economist and senior fellow at the Mises Institute. They discussed the recent pressure on gold and silver, Federal Reserve policy, government debt, the U.S. economy, and the risks of trying to create prosperity by expanding the money supply.

Mark Thornton said Kevin Warsh’s nomination as Federal Reserve chair helped trigger the latest downturn in precious metals. Warsh was viewed as the most hawkish of four potential candidates, he said, and his tough talk on inflation helped shift market expectations. Thornton added that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s statements and financial maneuvers contributed to the perception that officials were defending the dollar and bond markets.

Gold and Silver Face Pressure From Liquidity Needs

Thornton said the precious metals decline reflected more than government messaging. He pointed to higher oil prices and a weak global economy, which he said have forced individuals, companies, and governments to sell liquid assets to raise cash. In the Persian Gulf region, he said, reduced or disrupted revenues have added to those pressures, with gold among the assets being sold.

He described the combination of official rhetoric and liquidity demand as a forceful headwind for gold and silver. While he said he had expected Warsh’s nomination to weigh on the metals market, Thornton acknowledged that the scale of the downturn exceeded what he anticipated.

Federal Reserve Rate Policy and Government Debt

Thornton argued that interest rates are not as restrictive as many investors assume. He said the federal funds rate is only slightly above CPI inflation, leaving real interest rates low. He also said the Treasury and Fed have focused on short-term borrowing and Treasury bills while trying to contain longer-term yields, which influence mortgage and corporate borrowing costs.

Thornton estimated that the Fed had added about $400 billion to its balance sheet through short-term Treasury bills. He warned that shifting government borrowing from long-term bonds toward short-term debt could create risks, though he said he planned to examine the consequences more closely over the holidays.

The scale of federal borrowing, he argued, limits the Fed’s ability to keep rates high. Thornton cited roughly $2 trillion in new government borrowing and about $1.2 trillion in annual interest costs, alongside the refinancing of existing debt. In his view, the Fed will eventually face pressure to suppress borrowing costs to protect government finances and major banks.

Thornton Expects Lower Rates After Possible December Hike

Maharrey said he believed interest rates were more likely to be lower a year later than higher. Thornton agreed, despite market expectations for multiple rate hikes. He said forecasts had shifted toward the possibility of a single 25-basis-point increase in December, after Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller had recently discussed a possible 50-basis-point hike followed by three or four more increases in 2027.

Thornton expects few rate hikes as the stock market weakens and believes the Fed may later cut rates and inject money to stabilize markets. He said such interventions have occurred during previous business cycles, although they do not necessarily prevent a larger crash.

AI Investment, the Stock Market, and the Dot-Com Comparison

Thornton connected current financial risks to heavy investment in artificial intelligence, data centers, chips, and other advanced technologies. He said many firms had committed large amounts of cash and taken on substantial debt, while some projects were generating less revenue and higher costs than expected.

He compared the pattern to the dot-com bubble of the late 1990s. Maharrey noted that Nvidia had fallen about 50% from its high and that a recent initial public offering had moved below its issue price within days. Thornton said Federal Reserve interest-rate changes cannot fix weak business plans or make overextended investments profitable.

Thornton Questions the Strength of 4.3% GDP Growth

Maharrey cited a revised third-quarter GDP growth estimate of 4.3%, above the 3.5% expected figure, and asked why that growth did not match many Americans’ experience. Thornton called GDP a misleading aggregate when activity is concentrated in a few industries.

He said data centers, artificial intelligence, and semiconductor investment were driving a large share of reported growth. Such projects can boost GDP early through construction, land preparation, equipment purchases, and infrastructure spending, Thornton said, even when the benefits are concentrated among certain industries and workers.

Thornton also said many households were under financial strain. He claimed that roughly two-thirds of Americans were experiencing declining purchasing power or lacked confidence in the economy. He further cited estimates that about 30% of U.S. households did not always have enough food and that a similar share had negative net worth. These figures, he argued, show why strong headline GDP growth may not reflect conditions faced by many consumers.

Thornton Says Money Creation Cannot Produce Prosperity

Asked which economic fallacy he would eliminate, Thornton chose the idea that governments can print their way to prosperity. He traced criticism of that idea to Spanish scholastic scholars in the 1500s, who observed that the influx of gold and silver from the Western Hemisphere benefited the Spanish crown and court while weakening domestic productivity and industry.

Thornton said money creation can redistribute wealth without creating lasting prosperity. He argued that the lesson remains relevant to modern monetary policy and the Federal Reserve’s role in the economy.

data.title: Jobless Growth: What A Shrinking Workforce Means For Investors
data.description:
Jobless growth is usually a symptom of a weak economy, but this time the economy is growing due to productivity gains even as the workforce shrinks, which changes what investors should watch.

Key Takeaways

  • Real GDP grew by 2.2% in the year to mid-2026 while payroll employment grew just 0.3%. That is jobless growth by any definition.

  • Past episodes of jobless growth came after recessions, with unemployment between 5.6% and 9.1%. Today it’s happening mid-expansion with unemployment at 4.2%.

  • The workforce is shrinking. Participation among Americans 55 and older fell from 38.0% to 36.9% over the past year as boomers retire.

  • With fewer workers, growth has to come from productivity, which rose 2.2% over the past year, slightly above its long-run average of 2.0%.

  • For investors, weak payroll numbers alone are a poor recession signal now. Unemployment, layoffs, and the wealth effect matter more.

Here’s a combination that doesn’t usually last. Over the year to the second quarter of 2026, the U.S. economy grew 2.2% after inflation.1 Over roughly the same stretch, payroll employment grew 0.3%.2 Hiring averaged about 41,000 jobs a month over the 12 months through September, and four of those months were outright negative. Economists call this “jobless growth,” and it has a reputation as a warning sign.

The reputation is earned. Historically, jobless growth showed up after recessions, when companies squeezed more output from fewer workers and refused to hire until they had to. Add American Express announcing 3,500 job cuts on October 23 and the “recession is coming” crowd has plenty of material.3 However, when you look at who is actually leaving the labor force, this version of jobless growth tells a very different story, and it matters for how you read the next jobs report.

What Is Jobless Growth?

Jobless growth is exactly what it sounds like: the economy expands, measured by GDP, while employment barely moves. Normally, the two travel together because more output requires more workers. The chart below shows that relationship over six decades.

Notice in the chart above that the gold line usually tracks the black one. The gaps open in specific places: the early 1990s, the early 2000s, and the years after 2009. Each of those was a “jobless recovery.” Businesses had just lived through a recession, and demand was soft. Companies met rising orders by working existing staff harder rather than adding headcount.

Today’s gap looks similar on the surface. The difference is the unemployment rate sitting underneath it.

Source: BLS and BEA via FRED (GDPC1, PAYEMS, UNRATE). Two-year changes from Q2 (GDP) and June (payrolls). Calculations: RIA Advisors.

The last two rows are almost identical in growth and hiring. In 2011, jobless growth meant millions of people wanted work and couldn’t find it. In 2026, it means there are fewer people looking. Such is the distinction most of the “jobless growth” coverage misses, and it changes the investment conclusion entirely.

Hiring Stalled, But Unemployment Didn’t Rise

If weak hiring reflected weak demand for workers, unemployment would be climbing. It isn’t.

The unemployment rate was 4.4% in September 2025 and 4.2% in September 2026.4 Over the same year, the civilian labor force shrank by roughly 1 million people, from about 171.3 million to 170.3 million.5 When the pool of workers is shrinking, an economy doesn’t need many new jobs to keep unemployment steady. Oxford Economics has estimated that the “break-even” pace of job growth needed to hold unemployment stable is now close to zero.6

“So a 30,000 jobs print is fine now?” In isolation, it’s far less alarming than it would have been when the labor force was still growing, and new workers needed new jobs. What hasn’t changed is the direction of travel. A shrinking number is still a shrinking number, and as I’ve written before in The Sahm Rule, Employment, And Recession Indicators, it’s the change in unemployment, not the level of hiring, that has historically marked the turn.

The Workers Are Disappearing, Not The Jobs

The biggest reason for the shrinking labor force is demographic, and it’s been building for years.

Participation among Americans 55 and older climbed from 32.3% in 2000 to a peak of 40.7% in 2013. The leading edge of the baby boom was working longer than prior generations.7 That cohort is now leaving. Participation fell to 36.9% in September 2026, down from 38.0% just a year earlier. Slower immigration adds to it. Oxford Economics expected net inflows could fall to as little as 160,000 a year, from more than 3 million a few years ago.6

This is where I part company with the view that jobless growth is primarily an AI story. AI is real, and it plays a role, but the arrow runs the other way. When the labor force stops growing, businesses have only two ways to keep expanding: move the work offshore or replace it with technology. Automation is the response to a shrinking workforce, not the sole cause of it. Both responses are disinflationary over time, which fits the broader case I made in Bad Inflation Cures Itself. Good Inflation Doesn’t.

Where The Bears Have A Point

The other side of this argument has real merit. A “low-hire, low-fire” labor market is stable only as long as the “low-fire” part holds. Companies that aren’t hiring also aren’t building a cushion, and if layoffs start, there’s little momentum in hiring to absorb them.

“The labor market is the main firewall against a recession.” – Michael Pearce, Oxford Economics, quoted in Fortune, February 2026

There’s also a white-collar wrinkle. Gad Levanon of the Burning Glass Institute found that employment in finance, insurance, information, and professional services peaked in November 2022, even as output continued to rise. He called AI-enabled automation a “plausible contributor.”6 Those are well-paid jobs, and their incomes drive a disproportionate share of consumer spending. Throw in four negative payroll months in the past year, and the bears aren’t making things up. They’re reading the same data I am. They just draw a darker conclusion from a pattern that, so far, has kept unemployment near 4%.

Can Productivity Carry The Economy?

The math of growth is simple. Output equals the number of workers times what each one produces. If the first number is flat or falling, everything rides on the second.

As shown, productivity rose 2.2% over the year to the second quarter of 2026, slightly above its 2.0% average since 1965.8 That’s healthy, but it isn’t a boom, and it sets a ceiling. An economy with a flat workforce and 2% productivity growth has a speed limit of roughly 2% real growth, no matter what the AI headlines promise.

That ceiling matters for both sides of the market. For corporations, producing more with the same headcount improves margins. For households, it’s a mixed bag. Total wage income grows more slowly when the number of wage earners isn’t growing. Consumer spending then leans harder on raises for existing workers and on the stock market. Economist Byron Gangnes at the University of Hawaii estimated in October that the AI buildout’s direct contribution to growth has been small. The bigger effect, he found, has come through the stock market’s wealth effect on spending.9 I covered how fragile that channel can be in Wealth Effect Increases And Recession Risks.

“Jobless growth used to mean nobody was hiring. Now it means nobody is left to hire, and that is a very different problem.”

What Jobless Growth Means For Investors

I’m reasonably confident the shrinking labor force is a multi-year trend, not a blip. Boomers aren’t coming back to work. That makes jobless growth more likely to be the norm than the exception for the rest of this decade. What I’m less confident about is how smoothly the economy adjusts. A market that depends on asset prices for consumer spending is only as stable as those prices.

A few practical points follow from that view. First, stop reading weak payroll numbers as a recession signal on their own. With break-even job growth near zero, the unemployment rate and jobless claims are far better gauges. Second, separate the economy from earnings. Productivity-driven growth can support corporate margins even when hiring is flat. Third, keep an eye on the consumer. When incomes grow slowly, spending becomes more sensitive to a drop in the stock market, and that feedback loop runs in BOTH directions.

The trade-off is real. In my view, a disinflationary, slower-growth backdrop tends to favor high-quality bonds over aggressive growth bets, but it also means an economy with less room for error if a shock arrives. Such is the price of growing without new workers: steadier inflation, thinner cushions.

Bottom Line

Today's jobless growth reflects a shrinking workforce more than a collapsing economy, so investors should watch unemployment, productivity, and the wealth effect rather than the payroll headline.

The economy can keep growing without new workers. It just can’t afford to lose the ones it has.

Questions This Article Answers

What is jobless growth?

Jobless growth is a period in which the economy expands, measured by real GDP, while employment barely rises. In the year to mid-2026, real GDP grew by 2.2% while payroll employment grew 0.3%. Historically, it appeared after recessions, in the early 1990s, the early 2000s, and after 2009.

Is jobless growth a sign of a coming recession?

Not on its own. Past episodes saw unemployment between 5.6% and 9.1%, but in 2026 unemployment was 4.2% and falling, as the labor force shrank by roughly 1 million people. A rising unemployment rate is a more reliable warning sign than weak hiring.

Why is the US labor force shrinking?

Baby boomers are retiring, and immigration has slowed. Labor force participation among Americans 55 and older fell from 38.0% in September 2025 to 36.9% in September 2026, down from a peak of 40.7% in 2013.

How can the economy grow without adding jobs?

Through productivity, meaning more output per hour worked. Nonfarm productivity rose 2.2% in the year to mid-2026, slightly above its 2.0% average since 1965. With a flat workforce, that productivity rate sets a rough ceiling on real growth.

Sources & Notes

  1. U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, Real Gross Domestic Product (GDPC1), via FRED. Q2 2025 to Q2 2026 change calculated by RIA Advisors. Accessed Oct. 25, 2026.

  2. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, All Employees, Total Nonfarm (PAYEMS), via FRED. June 2025 to June 2026 change and the 12-month average through September 2026 calculated by RIA Advisors. Accessed Oct. 25, 2026.

  3. Yahoo Finance, “Stock market today,” market coverage of October 23, 2026, reporting American Express plans to cut about 5% of its workforce, or 3,500 roles.

  4. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, The Employment Situation, September 2026, released October 2, 2026, and Unemployment Rate (UNRATE) via FRED.

  5. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Civilian Labor Force Level (CLF16OV), via FRED. Household survey levels include annual population control adjustments each January, so year-over-year changes in levels are approximate. The direction matches the participation data.

  6. Jason Ma, “Jobless expansion,” Fortune, February 13, 2026, citing Oxford Economics (Michael Pearce) and the Burning Glass Institute (Gad Levanon).

  7. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Labor Force Participation Rate, 55 Years and Over (LNS11324230), via FRED. Accessed Oct. 25, 2026.

  8. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Nonfarm Business Sector: Labor Productivity (OPHNFB), via FRED. Average annual change since 1965 calculated by RIA Advisors. Accessed Oct. 25, 2026.

  9. Byron Gangnes, “Would we be in a recession without AI?” University of Hawaii Economic Research Organization (UHERO), October 21, 2026.

  10. Replication note: All four charts and the comparison table were built from FRED series GDPC1, PAYEMS, UNRATE, CLF16OV, LNS11324230 and OPHNFB, pulled October 25, 2026. Growth rates compare second-quarter (GDP, productivity) and June (payrolls) values. Monthly payroll changes for July, August and September 2026 match the revised figures in the BLS September Employment Situation. The 2.2% real GDP figure matches the four-quarter growth rate cited by UHERO.

data.title: Micron Stock Is Highly Undervalued As The Wyckoff Theory Takes Shape
data.description:
Micron stock has slipped into a bear market this month and now appears to be in the Wyckoff theory's markdown phase, even as its key valuation metric has fallen to bargain levels. MU was trading at $601, about 52% below its year-high. So, is this a good time to buy the dip, or should investors sell the rip?

Micron stock has become highly undervalued

In theory, companies that are seeing substantial revenue and profit growth should receive premium valuations. Some of the most popular companies that have always had a premium valuation are Walmart, Costco, and Shopify. 

Micron, however, is doing the opposite. Its revenue growth is soaring, and analysts expect the momentum will continue. The most recent results showed that its fourth-quarter revenue jumped by 379% to $54.2 billion, with its annual figure hitting $133.2 billion. Most of this growth was in its DRAM division, which made $39.8 billion. 

Micron is also a highly profitable company, with the gross margin of all its businesses being over 80%. Its total gross profit margin rose to 87%, much higher than most companies, including Nvidia. 

Most importantly, analysts believe that the company has more room for growth. For example, the first-quarter revenue is expected to hit $61 billion, while the second-quarter figure will soar to $66 billion. Its annual revenue is expected to jump by 106% to $275 billion. 

For a company experiencing this growth, its valuation metrics are significantly low. For example, the forward price-to-earnings ratio stands at just 3.43, much lower than the sector median of 18. 

Similarly, the company has one of the highest rule-of-40 metrics. This multiple is calculated by adding its revenue growth and its profit margins. Micron has a forward revenue growth of 106% and a profit margin of 64%, giving it a multiple of 170%. 

These metrics explain why the company is planning to accelerate its share repurchases in the near term. Its plan is to start a $35 billion program in December when the buyback restrictions end. Share buybacks help to boost a company’s earnings per share by reducing its outstanding shares.

Micron is facing risks

Therefore, the falling Micron stock price and cheaper valuation is happening because of the rising risks in the industry. One of the main risks is that the AI bubble may burst soon. The AI Stock Bubble Index has remained above 60.

There are also concerns that some AI data center companies will find it hard to survive as financing in the industry dries out. Elon Musk has warned that over 200 neocloud companies will collapse.

These fears have risen after the recent Anthropic IPO, in which the company raised over $100 billion. Its stock has plunged afterwards. OpenAI has also struggled in its fundraising. It recently raised $11 billion, much lower the $30 billion it was aiming for. 

There is also a risk that the memory supercycle will end in the coming months or years. Historically, this business is usually made up of major boom-and-bust cycles.

Micron share price is in the markdown phase

The weekly chart shows that MU stock has formed the classic Wyckoff Method. It remained in a consolidation phase for years, a sign that it was in the accumulation phase. 

The stock then entered the markup phase mid-last year and then started its upward trend, eventually reaching a record high of $1,255. Now, there are signs that it has dropped into the markdown phase, which is characterized by panic selling.

Therefore, the stock will likely continue falling in the near term. The next key level to watch will be at the 50-week moving average of $523.

data.title: Ethereum Glamsterdam Upgrade Cleared For December 15 Test: Will ETH Rally Like After Pectra?
data.description:
On Thursday, November 26, Ethereum’s core developers agreed to take the Ethereum Glamsterdam upgrade to its final public test on December 15, keeping a disputed gas rule exactly as written. The test runs on Hoodi, the network developers use as a dress rehearsal for mainnet.

It comes seven weeks later than planned. An October test was called off after a security firm warned that the new charges could change how programs already running on Ethereum behave. Developers now point to a mainnet launch in late January or early February, though no date is fixed yet.

ETH barely moved on the news. It trades at $1,730, down 42% since January 1. The Fear & Greed index sits at 12, deep in extreme fear, and traders have heard plenty of upgrade stories before.

So does a hard fork still move the ETH price?

Why Was the Ethereum Glamsterdam Test Delayed Until December 15?
The Gas Rule That Delayed the Test

The call summary on Ethereum Magicians records a “rough consensus” among execution teams to ship the current spec unchanged. The fight was over EIP-8037, a rule that adds a separate charge on anything that creates new permanent data on Ethereum, such as a new account or storage slot.

The goal is to stop the “state,” the database every node has to keep, from growing without limit. The price is steep. Creating a new contract today has a flat base cost of 32,000 gas. Under EIP-8037, the storage charge alone would be 183,600 gas, before regular fees.

That change is what worried auditors. ChainSecurity replayed a year of real Ethereum activity and found about 200 problems across bridges, wallets, exchanges, staking services and oracles. Most can be fixed with a setting, but 24 need code upgrades. Ethereum Foundation developer Marius van der Wijden estimates that up to 15,000 of Ethereum’s roughly 90 million contracts could be exposed.

A last-minute plan to simplify how the charges are tracked was turned down. Teams have until December 15 to report serious problems and until January 10 for the rest. Client releases for node operators are due early next week.

What Other Changes Will the Ethereum Glamsterdam Upgrade Bring?

The gas rule grabbed the headlines, but the Ethereum Glamsterdam list in EIP-7773 is long. Two changes matter most for how the network runs.

The first is enshrined proposer-builder separation, or ePBS (EIP-7732). Today, validators who propose blocks mostly buy them from specialist builders. Outside relays sit in the middle of that deal. ePBS moves it into Ethereum’s own rules, cutting out the middlemen that most blocks now depend on.

The second is block-level access lists (EIP-7928). A block will list up front which accounts and storage it touches, so nodes can load data and check transactions in parallel instead of one by one. That is groundwork for raising Ethereum’s capacity later.

Smaller items will please wallets and exchanges. Plain ETH transfers will emit a log, making them easier to track, and the maximum contract size goes up. The Sepolia testnet already switched to Glamsterdam on October 6.

ETH Price After the Last Five Ethereum Upgrades

An upgrade like Ethereum Glamsterdam sounds like good news for the price. The record is more mixed. We measured ETH’s move from the open on each mainnet upgrade day to the close 30 days later and compared it with bitcoin over the same window.

ETH beat bitcoin in the month after three of the five upgrades. The best run came after Pectra in May 2025, when ETH jumped 36% in 30 days while bitcoin added 8%. Shapella, which unlocked staked ETH in April 2023, and Fusaka last December also came out ahead.

The two misses were the most hyped launches. ETH fell 22% in the month after the Merge in September 2022, while bitcoin lost 6%. Dencun followed a 59% run-up in the month before it went live, and ETH then gave back 19%.

data.title: Is Trend Still Your Friend?
data.description:
Trend following is one of the oldest and most persistent anomalies in finance. The evidence that recent winners continue to outperform recent losers has been documented across virtually every liquid asset class, stretching back at least two centuries. It stands in direct opposition to the Efficient Market Hypothesis, yet it has survived out-of-sample testing, multiple market regimes, and decades of institutional capital deployed to exploit it.

However, something changed around 2008-09. A July 2026 paper, “Is Trend Still Your Friend? A Microstructural Account of the Demise of Short-Term Trend-Following,” by Jutta Kurth, Zoltan Eisler, Adam Rej, and Jean-Philippe Bouchaud, takes on a puzzling development in systematic investing: why short-term trend-following, reliable for decades, essentially stopped working after the Global Financial Crisis, while longer-horizon trend signals kept delivering. Their answer is not what most practitioners have assumed.

The Puzzle

The authors point to the SG CTA Index — the standard industry benchmark for large commodity trading advisors. After roughly a decade of steady gains, the index has been flat to negative for the better part of fifteen years, rescued only by two macro-driven episodes in 2014 and during the COVID shock.

Rebased) SG CTA Index, 2000–2025. Data courtesy of Société Générale Prime Services & Clearing.

The results are hypothetical results and are NOT an indicator of future results and do NOT represent returns that any investor actually attained. Indexes are unmanaged and do not reflect management or trading fees, and one cannot invest directly in an index.

The following chart shows the 5-20 day exponentially weighted (more weight given to the more recent days and less to the older days, with the weights decaying exponentially) moving average (EWMA).

The results are hypothetical results and are NOT an indicator of future results and do NOT represent returns that any investor actually attained. Indexes are unmanaged and do not reflect management or trading fees, and one cannot invest directly in an index.

Using their own methodological proxy built from about 100 liquid futures contracts across commodities, equity indices, currencies, and government bonds spanning 1995–2025, the authors confirm the same pattern with far more resolution.

Four empirical facts anchor the analysis and constrain any credible explanation:

  1. The break is abrupt — a regime shift, not a gradual decay of alpha.

  2. It is speed-dependent — fast trend signals (days to weeks) were hit hardest, while slow trend signals were largely unaffected.

  3. It is asset-class heterogeneous — equity indices and currencies were hit hard; yields and most commodities were largely spared.

  4. There has been no recovery, despite meaningfully improved liquidity and reduced CTA participation since 2018.

Four Candidate Explanations, Three of Which Fail

The authors test four hypotheses for what broke.

Capacity constraints. The idea that too much capital chasing the same signal eroded returns doesn’t hold up on close inspection. CTA industry assets grew through the 2000s and didn’t peak until 2022 — years after trend profit and loss (P&L) had already gone flat, the wrong sequencing for a crowding story. Liquidity in these markets rose sharply after 2018, which should have relieved any capacity constraint, yet performance never recovered. And when the authors recompute returns using same-day execution — effectively removing a full day of market impact and the associated costs — fast-signal performance is still flat after 2008. If capacity and execution costs were the culprit, stripping those costs out should restore profitability. It doesn’t. That’s an important clue: something happened to the underlying signal, not just the cost of harvesting it.

Electronification of futures markets. The shift from floor trading to electronic order books is a popular culprit, but the timing and sequencing don’t match. Electronification was gradual; the P&L break was sudden. Equity futures electronified more than five years before the break; interest-rate futures electronified early, yet never degraded at all.

A shift in CTA-versus-order-flow dynamics. The authors also examine whether a change in how CTA trades interact with aggregate market order flow explains the pattern. It doesn’t map cleanly onto which asset classes degraded and which didn’t.

The Variable That Actually Matters: Volatility-Normalized Tick Size

Having ruled out the usual suspects, the authors identify the variable that cleanly separates contracts whose trend signals survived from those that didn’t: the tick size of a contract, scaled by its volatility. Sorting the futures universe into “small-tick” and “large-tick” halves each month produces a stark dichotomy. Short-term trend P&L on small-tick contracts collapsed to essentially zero after 2008 across every signal speed tested. On large-tick contracts, performance barely budged — continuing to accrue at close to the pre-2009 rate even at the fastest signal horizons.

Notably, sorting by liquidity instead of tick size — despite the two being correlated — does not reproduce this clean separation. Nor does sorting by asset class on its own; the asset-class pattern turns out to be a byproduct of the fact that equity indices and currencies happen to cluster in the small-tick tier, while bonds and most commodities cluster in the large-tick tier.

Two further cuts of the data corroborate the framework. Trend gains have always been concentrated in low-volatility periods (a long-documented pattern known as the LeBaron effect—a negative (inverse) relationship between volatility and serial correlation of returns: when volatility is high, serial correlation tends to be low, and when volatility is low, serial correlation tends to be higher—and small-tick contracts continue to behave like large-tick contracts specifically during those low-volatility stretches — exactly what you’d expect if the ratio of tick size to volatility, not tick size alone, is what matters. And when the data is split by the magnitude of daily returns, the P&L earned on small, quiet trading days has been essentially untouched by the entire episode. It’s specifically the large, high-conviction directional moves — the ones that used to be trend-following’s bread and butter — where profitability vanished on small-tick contracts.

The Mechanism: A Broken Feedback Loop

Here the paper offers its most interesting contribution. The authors argue that trend following isn’t simply a static anomaly that traders harvest — it’s sustained by a self-reinforcing feedback loop. Trend signals prompt directional trades; those trades push prices further in the signal’s direction through market impact; that price movement sustains or strengthens the signal for the next trader to act on. Profitability and the very existence of the trend anomaly are, in this telling, two sides of the same coin. Break the loop, and both profitability and the signal itself should decay together — not just the harvest, but the underlying pattern.

What broke the loop, in the authors’ account, is the post-crisis takeover of market making by high-frequency trading firms operating on tight, flat-inventory mandates rather than the bank-affiliated and proprietary desks of prior decades that were willing to hold overnight risk. HFT market makers are structurally disinclined to absorb the kind of large, predictable, directional flow that CTA rebalancing generates—the literature on this point (HFTs withdrawing liquidity in front of large institutional orders) is well established.

That withdrawal happened across both tick-size tiers, but its consequences diverged sharply based on order book structure. Small-tick order books are inherently sparse — the economics of queue priority mean depth is naturally thin, so when HFT liquidity providers pulled back, there simply wasn’t enough residual depth left for trend followers to execute without materially “walking the book.” Faced with that cost, trend followers appear to have structurally disengaged from fast signals in those contracts — and once that flow disappeared, so did the impact-driven reinforcement that had been sustaining the trend signal in the first place. Large-tick order books, by contrast, are inherently dense, with meaningful resting depth at multiple price levels; residual liquidity there remained sufficient for trend followers to keep executing much as before, the loop kept turning, and both the signal and its profitability survived.

The authors also examined whether switching from aggressive market orders to passive limit orders offers an escape route on small-tick contracts. It doesn’t. A resting limit order tied to a trend signal gets filled preferentially in the wrong states of the world—filled when the market moves against the position, missed when it runs in the signal’s favor—which simply relabels the cost as missed opportunity rather than slippage. And passive orders, by definition, don’t generate the aggressive flow that feeds the self-reinforcing impact loop in the first place. There’s no execution style that sidesteps the underlying microstructural shift.

A Few Caveats Worth Flagging

Before turning to takeaways, as Max Martone noted in his LinkedIn post on the paper, a few caveats are worth naming. Two of the four authors, Rej and Bouchaud, are affiliated with Capital Fund Management, a large systematic manager whose book leans toward diversified, large-tick trend exposure—a microstructural explanation that vindicates that positioning over a capacity/crowding story is, at minimum, convenient for the firm, even if that doesn’t make the finding wrong. The supporting evidence for the mechanism is also less tidy than the headline P&L break suggests: the paper dates the P&L collapse to roughly 2008-09, but the book-imbalance correlation offered as corroboration doesn’t flip until around 2010, the adverse-selection evidence doesn’t flatten until 2011, and the trade-imbalance correlation shift is dated to 2015—four different break points folded into a single causal story. The small-tick/large-tick dichotomy itself is softer than the headline charts imply: the authors’ own robustness checks show the relationship behaves more like a continuous gradient than a clean binary split, meaning some of the crispness in the main results owes to where the median split happens to fall each month. And the central causal claim—that a shift toward HFT market making specifically drove the change in liquidity provision—isn’t directly evidenced in the data; no HFT participants are identified, and the authors acknowledge they can’t distinguish a change in who is providing liquidity from a change in how existing providers behave. None of this overturns the paper’s core empirical finding, which is well documented: small-tick and large-tick contracts diverged sharply after 2008. It does mean the explanation for why is more provisional than the confident framing suggests.

Key Investor Takeaways

The degradation of short-term trend appears structural, not cyclical. The authors see no obvious mechanism by which it reverses absent a genuine change in market-making structure—new regulation, a new class of inventory-tolerant liquidity providers, or a shift in tick-size regimes. That’s a meaningfully different diagnosis than “the trade got crowded and will eventually work again.”

Not all trend is created equal. Longer-horizon trend signals have held up far better than short-horizon ones, and the driver isn’t asset class so much as the underlying market microstructure—specifically, whether a contract’s order book is naturally sparse or dense relative to its volatility. Investors evaluating CTA managers or trend strategies should pay attention to what signal speeds and instrument mix a given strategy relies on, rather than assuming “trend” is a monolithic exposure.

Capacity discussions should happen at a finer level than the industry aggregate. Because the binding constraint operates tier by tier rather than strategy-wide, a fund’s overall participation rate can look comfortably below historical norms while still being effectively capacity-constrained within the small-tick subset of its book.

This is a good reminder of a broader lesson in evidence-based investing: market structure evolves, and strategies whose returns depend on specific liquidity-provision arrangements can see those arrangements change beneath them. The rise of HFT market making has reshaped a lot more than equity market microstructure—this paper is a well-documented example of how it can quietly erode a return premium that had persisted for roughly two centuries.

As always, the paper leaves open questions the authors themselves flag—most notably how much of trend’s historical existence owes to this impact-driven feedback loop versus more traditional behavioral explanations like slow information diffusion or underreaction to news. That distinction matters for how durable slower-horizon trend premiums are likely to be going forward, and it’s an area worth watching as more research emerges.

data.title: Silver Takes The Lead After The Miners' Reversal
data.description:
Yesterday, I wrote that the miners' reversal and volume were "very bullish for the following week." The rally didn't wait.

At the moment of writing these words, December gold futures are at about $3,639, after moving up to $3,683.50 this morning, and December silver futures are at about $43.52, after a high of $44.30. On Wednesday, the day before Thanksgiving, they moved down to $3,425.20 and $37.955, respectively, and then they reversed.

Silver is now leading the rebound, but the mining stocks moved first.

The Miners Moved First

Yesterday's analysis was about Wednesday's reversal in the miners. The GDXJ, which holds junior mining stocks, moved below Friday's low and then closed 10.4 percent above its intraday low, its biggest intraday rebound since April 2020, on big volume. I wrote: "In my view, the size of the reversal and the size of the volume are very bullish for the following week."

This morning, the GDXJ opened at about $92, up from Wednesday's close of $87.66, while the GLD, which tracks gold, opened at about $333, up from $327.45.

One of my Gold Trading Alerts subscribers asked in the comments this morning whether it's time to take profits on the miners, since they're close to my profit-take level while gold and silver are still below their targets. It's a good question, and I'm happy to answer it here as well. In my view, the miners are likely to keep leading, and in today's Gold Trading Alert, I described how I'm adjusting the position for it.

The reason why the miners tend to turn first is worth a closer look.

Why the Miners Lead at Bottoms

Mining stocks are leveraged to the price of gold. A miner's costs don't drop when gold falls, so its profits fall faster than the gold price does, and they rise faster when gold rebounds. Take a miner that produces gold at a cost of $2,000 per ounce. At $3,500 gold, its margin is $1,500 per ounce. At $3,800 gold, it's $1,800, which is 20 percent more, while gold is less than 9 percent higher.

The miners are also stocks, and stocks are priced on what investors expect. When investors think that the worst is priced in, they buy the miners before gold turns.

November 2008 shows the same thing on a bigger scale. Between September 22 and October 24, 2008, the USD Index rallied about 13 percent, while the S&P 500 fell about 27 percent and the GDX about 53 percent. In November, the USD Index moved to new highs, and the S&P 500 fell below its October low, closing at 752.44 on November 20. But on that day, the GDX closed at $18.20, above its October 24 close of $17.80. The next day, it soared 26.5 percent. By the end of 2008, the GDX was at $33.88, about 90 percent above its October 24 close, while gold was about 20 percent higher.

At real bottoms, the miners lead gold higher, but it's a tendency, not a law. This week, the miners led what I view as a corrective upswing, and gold and silver followed.

Gold Reversed Right After Reaching My $3,500 Target

Gold's part of the story started a month ago. On October 30, I wrote: "With the first target reached, the next one is about $3,500." When I wrote it, December gold futures traded near $3,906. On Wednesday, they moved down to $3,425.20, about 12 percent lower, and reversed on the same day.

This morning, December gold futures moved up to $3,683.50, about $258 above Wednesday's low. Zooming in allows us to see clearly that gold broke above its declining, very short-term resistance line.

The dollar didn't help. The USD Index is at about 103.92, up from Wednesday's close of 103.67, and the 10-year Treasury yield rose to about 4.90 percent. Gold rallying while the dollar moves higher and interest rates rise is a bullish sign for the short term.

Silver is rallying even more than gold.

Silver Takes the Lead

Silver's long slide started at a price that I had named in advance. On January 27, I wrote that "we might see another attempt that takes silver to $120 or even a bit above it before a bigger decline". Silver topped almost exactly at $120, and on Wednesday, December silver futures moved down to $37.955, their lowest level since June 2025, about 68 percent below that top.

This morning, they moved up to $44.30, and they're now at about $43.52. Silver moves more than gold in both directions, and when it rallies faster than gold, the gold-to-silver ratio falls. On Wednesday, the ratio moved up to about 90 at the lows. This morning, it's at about 83.

Another subscriber asked in the comments on Wednesday whether the ratio, which was forming a topping candle that day, was worth keeping an eye on. Yes, it is. In declines, silver tends to fall faster than gold, and the ratio rises. In rallies, silver tends to outpace gold, and the ratio falls. So the ratio's reversal from about 90 fits the upswing in the precious metals sector.

There's one more thing that I'm watching. Silver's strength against gold often shows up right before short-term tops. Today, gold and the miners are rising along with silver, so that's not the same signal. If silver soars while gold and the miners lag, I'll view it as a sign that the upswing is maturing.

Where This Leaves Us

The miners reversed first, on Wednesday, and today, silver is leading gold higher, while the gold-to-silver ratio falls from about 90 to about 83. Gold is rallying even though the dollar and Treasury yields are moving higher. In my view, this is a corrective upswing within the medium-term decline, and it's likely to continue for now. In today's Gold Trading Alert, I described how I'm adjusting the position in the miners and what I plan to do after this upswing.

The miners moved first. Now silver is catching up.

data.title: The AI Economics Don’t Add Up: Does Your Family Need 1.6 Million 20-Page Papers A Year?
data.description:
I hate when news articles write up numbers in millions, billions, and trillions without putting them in any context that would make them understandable to their audience. News reporting should not be a fraternity ritual; it should be about conveying information. 

Yesterday, I wrote a piece explaining why I didn’t think the economics of the AI economy made any sense. The basic point was that the overwhelming majority of users did not need the frontier AI. They could get by just fine with the cheap AI available from China, and also from more basic models from OpenAI or Anthropic.

Taking this a step further, I thought it would be helpful to put the volume of cheap AI these companies would need to sell to make a profit in a context people might understand. Yesterday, I used the denominator of 20-page papers. I figure that most people reading my posts probably have an idea of the work involved in writing a 20-page paper. 

I pointed out that 1 million output tokens, the standard pricing unit, should provide enough AI to generate roughly 75 twenty-page papers. OpenAI and Anthropic both have models that sell AI at 50 cents per 1 million output tokens. (Chinese companies have even lower cost AI.) 

At a bare minimum, the AI giants would need $1 trillion a year to break even with their costs, and more likely somewhere around $1.5 trillion. If they are getting 50 cents per million tokens, and 1 million tokens will produce 75 twenty-page papers, then the lower figure would imply 150 trillion twenty-page papers worth of AI a year, while the higher figure would imply 225 million twenty-page papers worth. 

Since most people are not used to working with trillions, this number can be calculated as a per- household figure. There are roughly 137 million households in the country. The first number implies just under 1.1 million twenty-page papers’ worth of AI per household, while the second number implies somewhat over 1.6 million. 

These are obviously crude calculations, but they should give us a ballpark idea of the amount of AI that needs to be sold for the industry to be profitable. There are issues that can be raised in both directions. Our AI companies hope to be selling overseas and not just to the domestic market. That will increase their market some, but they have major competition, most obviously from China. Furthermore, Chinese AI companies are likely to get a substantial share of the US market, so it’s not clear in which direction this adjustment would go.

The most important factor goes in the wrong direction for the AI crew. AI is getting cheaper. If we look out two or three years to when the AI companies need to be raking in over $1 trillion a year, the cost per million tokens may be far less than the 50 cents used in these calculations. In that case, people will really need a lot of 20-page papers for the AI story to make sense.
